articles.title: Yu, 13, wins record-breaking first major gold medal
articles.summary: China’s Yu Zidi, 13, wins a record‑breaking 200m women’s butterfly gold at the Asian Games in Tokyo.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Yu won gold by over three seconds in Tokyo 
- Published 20 September 2026 
Chinese schoolgirl Yu Zidi lit up the opening day of the Asian Games with a record‑breaking 200m butterfly gold medal secured by a performance she described as "only so‑so". 
The 13‑year‑old claimed her first major gold in two minutes 05.08 seconds, an Asian Games record that took almost half a second off compatriot Zhang Yufei's mark from three years ago. 
Yu, who is strongly tipped to make an impact at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, won by over three seconds in Tokyo from her team-mate Chang Mohan. 
"It was only so-so," a smiling Yu said after receiving her medal, adding that her butterfly technique "is still slightly lacking". 
"I hope I can swim even faster. I improved my time by 0.9 seconds here, and I believe I will perform better next time," she continued. 
Yu, who will take part in two more individual events at the Asian Games, became the youngest ever swimmer to win a medal at the World Championships when she took bronze as a 12-year-old as part of China's 4x200m freestyle relay team last year.

articles.title: See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition
articles.summary: The winning video features tiny hair-like structures, called cilia, in the airways of a child with a rare genetic disease.
articles.full_text:
See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition
See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition 
Close 
Nikon's annual Small World In Motion competition is open to anyone around the world with an interest in film or time-lapse photography through a microscope. 
This year's winning video was magnified to 100 times in size, and featured tiny hair-like structures, called cilia, in the airways of a child with a rare genetic disease. 
It was submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, who used a series of complicated light waves to illuminate different parts of the sample in colour. 
Runners up in the competition included videos of a roundworm encountering a single-celled organism and microscopic jellyfish larvae suspended in droplets of water. Clips of bioluminescent algae and a tiny sea slug were among the highly commended.

articles.title: Why a new Pakistan-China border pact has irked India
articles.summary: A China-Pakistan border pact challenges India's territorial claims and deepens strategic concerns over disputed Kashmir.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Future Publishing via Getty Images Image caption, 
Chinese soldiers hold a field exercise in the snow near the Kunjerab Pass bordering Pakistan By Soutik Biswas 
India correspondent 
- Published 21 September 2026 
For decades, India has refused to recognise a Pakistan-China boundary in a disputed part of the Himalayas that Delhi claims as its own. 
But last week, Pakistan and China formalised a boundary in a remote part of the mountainous region, drawing a sharp response from Delhi. 
The two countries signed the Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission, an agreement which Pakistan described as a "significant milestone" that would deepen cooperation on border management, trade and connectivity between India's regional rivals. 
Delhi rejected the move as having no legal basis, saying it did not recognise any Pakistan-China boundary located in territory it claims as Indian. 
The announcement comes at a particularly sensitive moment. 
India and China are seeking to stabilise their relationship after years of military tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the disputed line separating their forces along much of their Himalayan frontier. At the same time, Beijing and Islamabad are deepening cooperation along a neighbouring stretch of the frontier that India also claims. 
"There is no boundary between Pakistan and China. We reject the so-called Joint Commission, which is without any legal basis," Indian foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said. 
Image source, Corbis via Getty Images Image caption, 
The commission concerns the Pakistan-China frontier, including the Shaksgam Valley 
The commission concerns the Pakistan-China frontier, including the Shaksgam Valley, a roughly 5,180 sq km tract that Pakistan ceded to China in 1963 but which India claims as part of its territory in Ladakh. 
India says the territory was part of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir and was illegally occupied by Pakistan before being ceded to China. The Indian government has never recognised the agreement and considers it illegal and invalid. 
This history explains the particular sensitivity of Wednesday's announcement. 
"Pakistan has no locus standi to enter into arrangements concerning Indian territory under its illegal and forcible occupation," the Indian foreign ministry said. 
Pakistan says Jammu and Kashmir remains a disputed territory, and argues that India therefore has no standing to challenge its 1963 boundary agreement with China. It regards the agreement as valid. 
Jabin T Jacob, professor at the Department of International Relations and Governance Studies at Delhi's Shiv Nadar University, said the new development represented the revival of an old mechanism rather than an entirely new arrangement. 
"A joint boundary commission is provided for in the 1963 Sino-Pak Agreement, the only issue at hand is the timing of its operationalisation," he told the BBC. 
He said there could be several reasons for the timing, including China's broader effort to demarcate its boundaries and a desire to institutionalise exchanges and movement along a frontier at a time when Pakistan's other borders have experienced conflict and instability. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
An Indian army convoy driving towards Leh on a highway bordering China 
Jacob said India should be "worried" by the development. More importantly, he said, the move appeared to disregard a provision in the 1963 treaty itself. 
Article 6 of the agreement provided for its renegotiation once the Kashmir dispute was settled with whichever country ultimately controlled the territory, Jacob said. 
For India, Jacob said, the problem is compounded by the international information environment. 
"China's relative dominance of the international media and information landscape - [with] CGTN, CRI, presence on social media - relative to India allows it to put forward its narrative and maps globally while India is limited to fulminations that other world capitals are likely to ignore," he said. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Indian Army vehicles drive on a road near a mountain pass in India's Ladakh region 
That concern is distinct from the practical management of the frontier itself. Pakistan and China already have extensive infrastructure and connectivity links across the region, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and the Karakoram Highway. 
Husain Haqqani, former Pakistani ambassador to the US and now a senior fellow at Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy and Hudson Institute, said the new commission was both practical and political. 
"It is a combination of both," Haqqani told the BBC. "It is a mechanism to enhance border and boundary cooperation, prevent illegal crossings and protect the strategic infrastructure tied to CPEC." 
He said it also served as a signal to India that Beijing continued to view Kashmir through the Pakistani prism. 
"China has never accepted India's position on Kashmir and China views Gilgit-Baltistan from the Pakistani, not Indian prism," Haqqani said, referring to the region in Pakistan-administered Kashmir that borders China and which India claims as part of its territory. 
Haqqani said Islamabad's position had evolved in response to developments in Indian-administered Kashmir. 
"Pakistan still maintains that the final status of Jammu and Kashmir is yet to be decided," he said. "But since India has made internal changes - for example, the abrogation of Article 370 - in its part of Kashmir, Pakistan sees no issue with simply institutionalising what has been de facto with China since 1963." 
Image source, Anadolu Agency/Getty Images Image caption, 
The Gwadar port, west of Karachi, is a key part of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor 
For Beijing, the arrangement also fits into a broader pattern of using its relationships with neighbouring states to manage and signal its position towards India. 
Haqqani said reassurance to Pakistan on Kashmir was of both strategic and geopolitical value to Beijing. 
"On the strategic front it further deepens ties with Pakistan and on the geo-strategic front it reinforces for India its fear of a two-front threat from China and Pakistan, which pleases Pakistan and benefits China." 
The timing of the statement, say experts, is also significant. 
"China always plans its decisions months, if not years, in advance so the decision to operationalise a joint boundary commission must have been made some time back," says Haqqani. 
"The release of this information was timed for after President Xi Jinping's recent Brics summit trip to send Pakistan a message of reassurance in the strategic partnership, and India a reminder that multilateral engagement does not translate into any change in China's vision for South Asia." 
But Jacob cautioned against interpreting every aspect of the development as a direct military move against India. 
"There aren't any immediate or apparent implications for the LAC as of now," he said. 
That suggests that the significance of last week's announcement may lie less in an immediate change to the disputed Himalayan frontier than in the gradual institutionalisation of arrangements that India has consistently rejected. 
India's position, Jaiswal said, remained "clear and consistent": any attempt to legitimise what Delhi considers Pakistan's illegal occupation of Indian territory is unacceptable and has no bearing on India's sovereignty. 
But Haqqani believes the dispute goes beyond the legalities of borders. 
"The key disagreement between India and China about the border and boundary is geo-strategic, not cartographic," he said. "So there is a limit to what border negotiations and border management mechanisms can achieve." 
Pakistan, he added, remained "China's secondary deterrent against India" - and Beijing's engagement with Islamabad would continue to send that message to Delhi.

articles.title: Nvidia boss rejects AI extinction fears as 'doomsday narratives'
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's comments come after warnings from AI researchers that the technology could lead to human extinction.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 21 September 2026 
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has described warnings that AI could lead to humanity's extinction by the next decade as "doomsday narratives". 
"2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that's going to be the end of the world", Huang said in an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner. 
Huang added: "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible." 
Warnings from researchers in recent weeks about potential risks posed by the technology escalated the debate about AI safety, with some industry executives calling for a slowdown in developing models. 
His remarks follow claims posted on social media by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI developers believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade". 
Coxon's concerns sparked debate about the technology's risks, including calls by top executives like Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman urging for AI's development to slow down. 
Huang said that such predictions are "not grounded in science", adding that it is in Nvidia's best interest to ensure the industry builds its products responsibly. 
"Our company's success is directly connected to the safe deployment of products and services," he said. "If we don't continue to do that, our value would be diminished." 
Huang suggested AI firms talking about a "slow down" could be seeking liability protections for harms their products may cause. 
"Go and read between the lines," he said. "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have, and I think that that's a problem." 
Huang's comments echo those from multiple people contacted by the BBC who have worked for companies including OpenAI, Meta, and DeepMind. 
In text exchanges and conversations, they said were sceptical of the idea that unchecked AI development would lead to tools that could kill people en masse.

Nvidia is a key player in the industry, developing cutting edge computer chips that are crucial for making AI models. 
The firm's most powerful chips face restrictions in China due to measures imposed by both Washington and Beijing. 
US export controls aim to slow China's military and AI progress, while Chinese regulations are designed to encourage reliance on domestically produced technology. 
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held talks in New York on Sunday as they try to strike deals on AI, tariffs and critical minerals. 
After the meeting, Bessent told reporters that the two sides had discussed setting up a new AI safety notification mechanism. 
It came as President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. 
Last week, Huang appeared at a UK summit hosted by King Charles , who warned tech leaders of the "existential dangers" of AI. 
"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," the King told the group. 
In the US, President Donald Trump has downplayed concerns about AI's risks . 
Trump made a surprise phone call to Huang while the Nvidia boss was speaking on stage at a tech conference in Los Angeles on 14 September. 
During the call, Trump criticised calls to slow the pace of AI development and dismissed fears as a "hoax".

articles.title: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
articles.summary: The BBC's Frank Gardner speaks to some of those who have fled the war by crossing the Red Sea to Djibouti.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees in Djibouti By Frank Gardner Security correspondent ,  Reporting from Markazi camp, Obock, Djibouti 
- Published 21 September 2026 
Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them. 
Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab Strait. 
After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN. 
"How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them." 
- 
UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham 
- Published 2 hours ago 
-

- Published 11 September 
Image source, Ed Habershon/ BBC Image caption, 
Ibrahim Issa escaped on his fishing boat with family and several goats 
As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen. 
He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in. 
In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. 
This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. 
Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. 
"We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee." 
Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. 
And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded. 
Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old. 
"What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically. 
"It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere." 
Image source, Ed Habershon/ BBC Image caption, 
More than 120,000 Yemenis are estimated to have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting 
Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate. 
Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi. 
He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears. 
"Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us." 
How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014. 
A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes. 
Image source, Frank Gardner/ BBC Image caption, 
"We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country," says Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed 
Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed. 
Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here." 
His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first, then food, water and an education. 
"As you see we just fled with our clothes, and left everything behind, because [in Yemen] there is no peace."

articles.title: Xhaka under investigation over Covid-19 certificate
articles.summary: Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is being investigated over an issue with his Covid-19 vaccination certificate.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Granit Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year By Ffion Wynne BBC Sport Journalist 
- Published 21 September 2026 
Switzerland captain Granit Xhaka is under investigation by Swiss prosecutors over allegations he obtained a forged Covid-19 vaccination certificate. 
The 33-year-old is alleged to have obtained the certificate in 2022, when it was a requirement in Switzerland for some travel abroad. 
The public prosecutor's office of the city of Lucerne confirmed the investigation was under way to determine whether any criminal behaviour took place in obtaining a "false or forged" certificate. 
The Sunderland midfielder, who was playing for Arsenal at the time, posted a statement on social media on Monday saying he had a "mistrust" towards the vaccine and had been "influenced by worries and uncertainty". 
He said: "In this troubled state of mind I acquired a vaccine certificate, instead of clarifying my unanswered questions in the proper way. 
"Today I see clearly, that this way was not correct. It was a mistake. I'm sorry. 
"I take responsibility for this decision, will engage with the process of establishing the facts and fully co-operate with the relevant authorities." 
The Swiss office of public health confirmed that while there was never a general legal requirement to obtain or hold such a certificate, it was needed for access to various activities, venues and travel, meaning that participation was restricted for anyone who did not possess one. 
These measures in Switzerland were in place until spring 2022. After that point, Covid-19 certificates continued to be issued, primarily to enable members of the public to meet entry requirements when travelling abroad. 
It is unclear what punishments Xhaka could face, but in 2023 the then Switzerland men's ice hockey coach Patrick Fischer was found guilty of using a fake Covid-19 certificate to work at the 2022 Winter Olympics ‌in Beijing. 
Fischer was fined 38,000 Swiss francs by a criminal court. In April this year, he was sacked from the Switzerland job and earlier this month, he was banned for four years by the International Ice Hockey Federation. 
The Swiss Football Association said Xhaka, the country's record appearance holder with 152 caps, had withdrawn from the Swiss camp for their upcoming Nations League matches against Scotland, North Macedonia and Slovenia following his statement. 
It added the decision to withdraw had been made jointly by the player and management and that they would discuss Xhaka's future with the team after the international window. 
Switzerland have away fixtures against North Macedonia and Scotland on 26 and 29 September, before facing Slovenia and North Macedonia at home in early October. 
Sunderland boss Regis le Bris refused to comment on the allegations following the Black Cats' defeat at Manchester City on Sunday. 
"It is not my area to speak about those problems or situations," he said. "My area is football. About football, he is really good." 
Xhaka captained Switzerland at the World Cup earlier this year, where they were knocked out in the quarter-finals by eventual runners-up Argentina.

articles.title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
articles.summary: Top US and Chinese officials held talks in New York on Sunday ahead of a Trump-Xi summit this week.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent/X Image caption, 
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met China's Vice Premier He Lifeng By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 21 September 2026 
Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday. 
Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York. 
The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week. 
AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach. 
"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks. 
He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade. 
A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November. 
The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment. 
Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI. 
Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people." 
The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries. 
In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears abouts its potential negative impact on humanity. 
Trump has largely dismissed those concerns , arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China. 
He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins." 
In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed. 
Those talks ended with an agreement that China would buy Boeing jets and US agricultural goods in exchange for lower tariffs.

articles.title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting
articles.summary: While Burnham praised the agreement, Lib Dem leader Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory for Trump.
articles.full_text:
Image source, EPA By Henry Moore 
- Published 20 September 2026 
Andy Burnham has hailed a deal between Denmark and the US to "strengthen security in the Arctic" after the two countries resolved a months-long feud over Greenland. 
The UK prime minister and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region" in a call on Sunday morning, Downing Street said. 
Nato previously said the agreement would help stabilise the region, while Trump declared Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic. 
Burnham's comments come as he is expected to meet Trump for the first time at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York this week. 
- 
Nato welcomes Greenland deal as Trump says it will give US 'permanent security control' 
- Published 2 days ago 
The agreement comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic Arctic location for defence purposes as well as its mineral wealth. 
No text of the agreement has been released, but Trump said in a Truth Social post that the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and meant it could "do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland". 
He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval". 
A No 10 spokesperson said in a readout of Sunday's phone call that Burnham and Frederiksen "welcomed the US's commitment to the region and underlined the strategic and shared importance of the High North for Euro-Atlantic security". 
The spokesperson added: "The prime minister congratulated Prime Minister Frederiksen and the Kingdom of Denmark on negotiating a deal benefiting the US, Greenland and Denmark, and said he would pass on his congratulations to President Trump." 
While Burnham praised the agreement, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey called it a "pretend" victory and a nearly identical to the existing agreement. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Greenlanders protested against Trump's ambitions for the territory in the country's capital, Nuuk, earlier this year 
"Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said during a Q&A at the Lib Dem party conference. 
"So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won." 
Trump had for months threatened to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. 
Following the announcement of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week. 
The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen. 
The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted. 
Burnham has spoken to Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intended to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home", including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says
articles.summary: Moscow's mayor says 450 drones were downed during the overnight barrage, in which two people died.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Moscow oil refinery seen on fire after Ukrainian drone attack By Jaroslav Lukiv   and   Dearbail Jordan 
- Published 20 September 2026 
Ukraine has fired its largest drone attack on the Moscow region, the mayor has said, hitting the city's main oil refinery and a residential building. 
Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called "the most massive" attack. The region's governor said at least two people were killed and 20 injured. 
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region with drones and missiles, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine". 
Ukrainian officials meanwhile said nine people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday. 
Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs. 
A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Andrei Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured. 
An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Governor Andrei Vorobyev added. 
Videos verified by the BBC on social media show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse. 
Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and the oil refinery - where Ukrainian military officials said three key units had been damaged. 
The site supplies more than a third of the Moscow region's fuel, according to the defence ministry in Kyiv, and some of its petrol, diesel and aviation fuel go to Russia's military. 
Ukraine's defence minister said attacking such facilities "directly undermines the enemy's ability to continue its war of aggression and supply its military formations". 
Sobyanin said the major attack was "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election, which was in its third day on Sunday. The vote is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and has been dismissed by critics as neither free, fair nor transparent. 
Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
A building in the Moscow region early on Sunday, which Russian officials said had been hit by a Ukrainian drone strike 
Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed. 
It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Saturday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko.

Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so. 
Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India. 
The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.

articles.title: Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
articles.summary: Political shifts in Germany are being watched closely in Europe and beyond, Katya Adler writes.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The German chancellor's political future hangs in the balance after bruising election defeats By Katya Adler Europe editor 
- Published 21 September 2026 
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker. 
The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them. 
The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield. 
At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began. 
German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems. 
He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks. 
The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament . 
Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well. 
It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist. 
The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The AfD, led by Tino Chrupalla and Alice Weidel, has surged in national opinion polls 
The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want. 
Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party. 
The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets. 
High time for political change, says the AfD. 
Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician. 
Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party. 
I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual. 
Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted. 
Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed. 
He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required. 
Figure caption, 
Why Merz is staying on as German chancellor after election 'disaster' 
But German patience is running thin. 
Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future. 
Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped. 
Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people. 
Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology. 
In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive". 
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect. 
Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
As the AfD squeezes the CDU on the right, the left wing Die Linke party attracts voters elsewhere 
Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget. 
When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable. 
Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example. 
This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech. 
Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels. 
The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and the hard left Die Linke too, with concern. 
These regional German votes come at the start of bumper election season across the EU, where all the big powers - (including France, Italy, Spain and Poland - go to the polls. 
Nationalist, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration parties are predicted to do well. And Beijing and Moscow are watching closely.

The successful candidate must win support from nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters 
View image in fullscreen 
The successful candidate must win support from nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters Analysis 
Race to be next UN secretary general could rest on US and China trade-offs
Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor, in New York 
Numerous possible last-minute entrants being discussed as current field of seven candidates struggle to garner support 
Numerous last-minute entrants in the race to become the new UN secretary general are being discussed amid concerns that the world powers may not be able to agree a successor to António Guterres from the current field of seven candidates. 
Three rounds of secret ballots have so far not produced an obvious frontrunner, with probably only three candidates regarded as still having a realistic chance of gathering the required support. 
The new leader, due to take office in January, will face an organisation at the start of a cost-cutting overhaul programme and seen as marginal to the major global conflicts. In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it? | Steve Bloomfield 
Read more 
But surveys still show strong international support for the institution among a public that blames world leaders as much as the UN itself for its recent failing. 
A survey by GeoPoll for the UN Foundation published last week found six out of 10 people trust the UN to deliver on the issues that matter to them, but 85% said they had heard nothing or little about the process to choose a new secretary general. 
The successful candidate must win the support of nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members of the council – France, the UK, China , Russia and the US. 
Achieving consensus among the permanent five is fraught given the breadth of political divisions. Guterres’s term ends on 31 December. 
Names being mentioned as potential late drafts include Lana Nusseibeh, the minister of state at the United Arab Emirates and a former UAE ambassador to the UN, and Sigrid Kaag, a former UN under secretary general and Dutch centrist politician. She was briefly the senior humanitarian and reconstruction coordinator for Gaza before joining the advisory committee to Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. 
Other candidates mentioned include Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the polyglot president of Kazakhstan, and, in deference to the US, Viktor Orbán, the former prime minister of Hungary, who is still much admired by Trump but reviled as a disruptive populist by many European leaders. 
Vuk Jeremić, a Serbian former president of the UN general assembly who came second behind Guterres in the 2016 race, has also been mentioned. 
View image in fullscreen 
Dutch politician Sigrid Kaag has been mentioned as a possible late entrant into the contest. Photograph: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP 
None of the speculated candidates have given any public indication they wish to be drafted. 
A communique at the end of this month’s Brics summit attended by 21 countries, of which 10 are full members, said: “We note that no woman has ever been elected for the role of secretary general, and only one national from Latin America and Caribbean, and only two nationals from Africa and Asia each have ever occupied this position.” 
Some would also resent a late candidate, regardless of their origin, entering the field since strenuous efforts have been made to democratise the selection process by holding regional and global hustings. The last general assembly president, Annalena Baerbock, has helped spearhead the attempt to open the selection process. 
But the need to avoid alienating any of the five, internally divided, veto-wielding security council members inevitably incentivises the candidates to issue slightly bland consensus-seeking statements at a time when the organisation needs firm leadership. All the candidates have said they would like to see the UN return to an active role as a peacemaker – a task often demanded by amateur US diplomats close to Trump. 
In the third and last straw poll of the 15 security council members on Friday, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica regained the lead after receiving nine “encourage” votes from the security council. She got five “discourage” votes and one “no opinion”. Her fear is that the discourage votes came from Russia and China, an opposition she would need to overcome. 
In the second straw poll on 21 August she had dropped behind Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett , a Guyanese politician who then came first – receiving eight encourage votes, three discourage and four no opinions. 
Last Friday, Rodrigues-Birkett maintained the eight encourage votes, but her discourage votes had risen from three to six. 
A third candidate, the Ecuadorian former finance minister María Fernanda Espinosa, is just about still a viable contender despite the numbers discouraging her reaching six last week, up from three in August. She has been calling for an early warning system inside the UN to help prevent wars, and for a secretary general more willing to take risks in mediation. 
View image in fullscreen 
Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica regained the lead in the last poll but received five ‘discourage’ votes. Photograph: Santiago Mazzarovich/AFP/Getty Images 
It will not be until later in the process – when colour-coded balloting reveals if a vote is from a permanent member of the security council or not – that it will be clear whether a candidate faces an insurmountable barrier. 
In reality the decision may turn on the horse-trading between the US president and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and whether Trump accepts that China cares more about the UN’s future than him, and that may mean accepting a candidate that China wants and the US can tolerate. 
The Trump administration appears to have softened some of its scepticism towards the UN under the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz. The US not only provided $1.8bn (£1.35bn) in additional humanitarian funding in March but also recently sent $827m in dues, admittedly less than a quarter of what it owes the cash-strapped organisation. 
Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile and a human rights campaigner, became the first candidate to drop out of the race at the weekend after she received only one encouragement in last week’s poll.

articles.full_text:
There is likely to be more to come from Donald Trump – even if his wings are clipped on the domestic front after the midterm elections. Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty Images 
View image in fullscreen 
There is likely to be more to come from Donald Trump – even if his wings are clipped on the domestic front after the midterm elections. Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty Images 
Whiplashed middle powers seek new alliances as Trump rages on world stage
While world leaders prepare for annual UN gathering, shifts in the global order continue in the face of a disruptive American president 
I n the event of a midterms election battering, it is possible that a deflated Donald Trump , constrained by a Democrat-controlled Congress, will gradually have to face up to the indignity of irrelevance. 
While continuing to sign off Truth Social posts with his usual, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, no one will actually be paying much attention. His meandering press conferences will no longer be carried live by TV networks. The Republican party will move on to the question of his successor. Trump could announce he had changed the name of the Champs-Élysées to Sunset Boulevard and even Google Maps will stifle a yawn. He would become that most pitied of political animals, the lame duck. 
Yet somehow this scenario does not seem to fit the Trump personality, the US media landscape or indeed the recent history of other presidential endings. Just before completing their own terms in office, George W Bush launched the Iraq war “surge”, Bill Clinton got China into the World Trade Organization and Ronald Reagan helped end the cold war. 
Trump will also surely rage against the dying of the light. 
View image in fullscreen 
Donald Trump speaking at the White House on 30 January 2025 about the mid-air crash between an American Airlines plane and a military helicopter in Washington. Photograph: China News Service/Getty Images 
Many observers, including the former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton and the former UK foreign secretary David Lammy, predict Trump will concentrate even more on his disruptive foreign policy after November’s midterms, seeking to go even further and faster. Potential legislative gridlock in Congress would block him off from domestic initiatives, so the thinking goes, but much less so foreign policy. 
The likes of António Guterres, attending his final UN general assembly as secretary general this week, who have tried to impress on Trump that the US could achieve more in alliance with others than alone, are likely to receive short shrift. 
Those hoping for a return from the orderless world to one of order, loosely built around a set of recognisable values, are likely to be disappointed. In short, there is more to come. 
T hat assessment is accelerating a trend across the world of countries forming a complex web of diplomatic, military and trading alliances designed to act as protective shields from an unpredictable and predatory US president. These hedging alliances, born out of fear of entrapment or of abandonment, are springing up across the globe, changing the matrix of diplomacy, often but not always in favour of the other superpower of the age, China. 
John Bew, a foreign policy adviser to four former British prime ministers, describes the process as the creation of “a sub-threshold international order”. 
As Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, urged in a speech at Davos in January, the middle powers are reorganising. The trend is most obvious among former US allies. 
Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, said: “The world is moving from a situation where countries saw themselves within the context of an alliance system – ‘How do we plug and play and make it all about interoperability with American grand strategy?’ – towards one where the primary goal is: ’How do we hedge and how do we make sure that we can defend ourselves if America isn’t there?’” 
Wherever one looks it is the alliances in which the US does not feature – from Brics to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) – that are thriving and deepening. 
The recent Brics summit in Delhi ended with a declaration 140 dense paragraphs long that centred on how sovereign states can insulate their economies, supply lines, and payment infrastructures from weaponised western financial networks. The aim was to show that the “global south” can shape rules without turning into an anti-American alliance. “The operational strategy does not aim to eradicate the dollar overnight,” the Indian commentator Navroop Singh explained, “but to construct a parallel, non-dollar pipeline through which bilateral commerce, especially in strategic commodities like oil, gas, agriculture, and critical minerals can flow unhindered by extraterritorial oversight of the United States.” 
At this month’s SCO meeting at Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan, China’s president, Xi Jinping, said: “The overwhelming majority of countries do not subscribe to power politics, do not want conflict and confrontation, and do not wish to remain closed off and left behind. Instead, they aspire to secure an equal place on the world stage through their own development and international cooperation.” 
Formed to manage border disputes among former Soviet states, the SCO’s activities long ago expanded to include an economic dimension fostering connectivity, trade and investment. 
View image in fullscreen 
Xi Jinping speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan on 1 September. Photograph: Zhai Jianlan/Xinhua/AP 
By contrast, in the groupings that the US dominates, such as the G7 and Nato, the recent key ambition has been to shape an agenda that avoids a Trump walkout. Success is measured according to whether the west avoids public disintegration. 
Sometimes these new ad hoc alliances are relatively mundane. Some operate inside existing institutions, others involve the creation of specific new cooperation trading mechanisms such as memorandums of understanding on trade in critical minerals or the development of new overlapping institutions. In the case of the UK, the Chatham House thinktank suggests as many as six different mini-alliances could be formed to build submarines and air engines, share critical minerals, or promote free trade. 
View image in fullscreen 
Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (left), with Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (centre) and Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, meeting in Mecca. Photograph: Turkish Presidency Press Office/AFP/Getty Images 
The biggest and most striking recent manifestation of this new order came in the Middle East on 7 August, when Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca pact – a defensive military alliance that for some is about ending the dependency on the US military umbrella, and for others combatting Iran. Either way, it is likely to rewrite the Middle East’s security architecture. 
Trita Parsi, from the US foreign policy thinktank the Quincy Institute For Responsible Statecraft, said: “If you sit in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries right now, you must feel tremendously vulnerable because you have put all your eggs in the American security basket and it turned out not only not to work, but it was supposed to be a guarantee that others would be deterred from attacking you. Instead, the US started a war against the wishes of most Gulf countries and within that war, the entire infrastructure of the US bases turned out not to be a deterrent, but a magnet.” 
Not only were exposed bases pummelled by Iranian missiles and drones to the point, in the words of Gen David Petraeus, that they became “no longer viable”, the Gulf states also discovered the US was prepared to allow Israel to bomb Qatar’s capital, Doha, in the hope of assassinating the Hamas leadership. It was the first such attack on a GCC state, and changed the GCC’s security calculations as to whether Iran or Israel ultimately was the primary threat in the region. 
View image in fullscreen 
A building damaged in Doha, according to an Israeli official, after an Israeli attack on Hamas leaders on 9 September 2025. Photograph: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/Reuters 
The US insists in public it will reinvest in better-protected bases and will shortly lay out a postwar vision in which the US remains indispensable to the Gulf’s security. But Majed al-Ansari, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Gulf nations cannot rely solely on the US and other international alliances for their security. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward.” 
Parsi admitted it was not clear what kind of tree would grow out of the seed sown in Mecca. “Is it another bloc formation that at its core divides the region, leading to rivalry and confrontation, or is it, as the Turks insist, an open constellation that is not targeting anyone but based on collective security?” 
Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, meanwhile, requires foreign investment, tourism and reliable energy routes. Endless wars promoted by Israel and not constrained by the US for purposes not in Saudi Arabia’s long-term interest are a ball and chain on the Saudi economy. 
In all this, there are deep implications for India, a country dependent on the Middle East for nearly 60% of its crude oil and about 70% of its liquefied natural gas requirements. It may need to form its own hard power security partnerships in the region. 
Writing in Foreign Affairs magazine , Marc Lynch, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University, asked recently: “If Washington could not even be counted on to consult its allies, defeat its adversaries, or protect its partners from the fallout of its regional misadventures, then what good were its promises? The fundamental bargain the United States offered has crumbled, and it will not be easily rebuilt”. 
The same set of questions has been posed in Europe, leading to calls for a more Europeanised Nato, most often perceived as an alliance of its five main military powers, a constellation that conveniently bypasses Brexit and would allow Germany, France, Italy, Poland and the UK to work together to face the Russian threat, assuming these democracies next year remain led by forces opposed to Putin’s authoritarianism. 
View image in fullscreen 
(Clockwise from left to right) Western leaders attend a meeting at the 62nd Munich Security Conference in February in Germany. Photograph: Getty Images 
Debate about this alliance, promoted at the Munich Security Conference, is driven by the twin fears of the hybrid war conducted by Moscow and the US plan to leave the conventional defence of Europe to the Europeans. Trumpites treat Europeans primarily as trade competitors and sometimes a civilisational threat, not allies. No one can assume that the US would come to Europe’s defence in the event of a Russian attack. Not surprisingly, Poland, the Baltics and Scandinavia have since 2022 increased their defence spending by 71%, 134% and 126% respectively. The call to buy European arms is growing. 
Such is the concern about where Trump could go next after his threats to Greenland, that some European diplomats privately express relief that the US was unable to repeat the success of Venezuela in Iran. There is no love for the Iranian government, save for its ability to remind Europe of the risks inherent in relying on US military and technological supremacy. 
T he country that most acutely faces the American dilemma is of course Canada . Now entering an asymmetric trade war with the largest and most powerful country in the world, it has little doubt about the rupture it is confronting. Bob Rae, a former Canadian ambassador to the UN, recently wrote: “Canada’s nextdoor neighbour is a predatory hegemon [that] tears up treaties, makes a mockery of international law and clearly has a different concept of the relationships between might and right, and between law, morality and self-interest.” 
But there was an ambiguity deep in Carney’s Davos message. Was he seeking simply to locate new markets blocked by US tariffs, or was he trying to build a network of countries – a third bloc – with like-minded liberal values? Rae argued that for the middle nations alliance to thrive, Carney needed to be clearer about what values Canada stands for, including upholding international law. He wrote: “We can succeed in defeating such aggression only if we are willing to extend economic, political and military support to other countries and jurisdictions facing similar attacks and threats.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, addresses the European parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters 
In his speech to the European parliament this week while trying to provide the cure to the harsh realities his Davos speech diagnosed, Carney argued that associate membership of the EU would not just be about economics, but an affinity of deep-rooted shared values that implicitly Canada no longer shared with the US. But the rules-based EU does not give access to its markets readily, and the big vision could soon become entangled in the small print Brussels adores. 
Sometimes this crisis of the west is seen as an exclusively European phenomenon. But South Korea finds itself in a similar place to Canada. Ulchi Freedom Shield, the annual joint military exercise that the US and South Korea held to counter the North Korean threat, was abruptly scaled back by Washington just before it was due to begin in August. Trump ordered the drills cut from 11 days to five, citing costs, his desire to improve relations with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, and South Korea’s reluctance to support his war on Iran. The decline in US military stocks due to the Iran war has hardly helped.

It has intensified a debate in South Korea , and in Japan, about pursuing independent nuclear weapons, especially given the apparent indifference of the US and the international community to North Korea’s programme. 
The friction has given Xi a golden opportunity to promote China to South Korea and Asia as the more reliable ally. 
Optimists such as Kurt Campbell, who under Joe Biden’s presidency latterly as deputy secretary of state did more than anyone to reconstruct American alliances across Asia after the Trump first term, insists his task can be repeated. Thirteen-year-old swim sensation sets women’s 200m butterfly record at Asian Games
Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi wins the first major title of her young career – but says her performance was ‘only so-so’ 
The 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi set an Asian Games record as she scorched to gold on Sunday’s first full day of competition. 
The schoolgirl, who turns 14 next month, took the women’s 200m butterfly crown in a Games-record 2min 05.08sec. 
It was the first major title of her young career, less than two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics. 
“It was only so-so,” a smiling Yu said after receiving her medal.

Swimming is one of three sports at the Games taking place in Tokyo, where a typhoon is due to blow in, with the rest of the Games unfolding in Nagoya and Aichi prefecture. 
China is expected to be the pre-eminent power in the pool, on day one clinching six of the seven titles on offer. 
The Games were officially opened on Saturday by Emperor Naruhito. 
For the next two weeks, athletes will compete in more than 40 sports before closing on 4 October. 
The Games has 2028 Olympics places up for grabs but have been dogged by a series of problems in the buildup. 
Accommodating the more than 11,000 athletes and 6,000 officials has stretched organisers to the limit after they decided not to have a traditional athletes’ village to save money. Competitors are instead staying in a combination of temporary container-style huts, hotels and on the Costa Serena cruise ship. 
The International Olympic Committee president, Kirsty Coventry, called the temporary huts “beautiful” on Sunday after looking around – but conceded they were “a little tighter” than similar accommodation at the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics this year. 
Japanese organisers will be desperate for the sport to take over from a troubled lead-in that included complaints about the accommodation and a shortage of rooms. 
However, an incoming typhoon that soaked Tokyo on Sunday could cause more problems. 
The Tokyo venue hosting equestrian was closed because of the weather. The competition is now due to start on Tuesday, a day later than originally planned. 
The full force of Typhoon Dujuan will not be felt until Monday, with Tokyo expected to be hit with strong winds and heavy rain. 
Nagoya will not be in the storm’s immediate path but wet weather is forecast there too. 
Iran celebrated wildly after beating China 79-70 to win men’s basketball bronze. 
South Korea won basketball gold, silencing the home crowd with a 67-57 win over Japan. 
In other sports, Smriti Mandhana became the highest run-scorer in women’s T20 international cricket as India crushed Bangladesh by 114 runs in the semi-finals, with fellow opener Shafali Verma hitting her maiden hundred. 
India will face Sri Lanka in Tuesday’s final, unless the weather intervenes.

‘People had naive expectations’: How MeToo has changed in China
On Friday, MeToo journalist Sophia Huang Xueqin was released from prison. She returns to a landscape changed by censorship, and a new generation of feminists 
W hen Jasmine, a once active member of China’s MeToo movement, organises feminist activities in Beijing, she often does so under the guise of an art or cultural event. She avoids publicising them on social media, instead sharing details privately in her personal circle. Being a woman in China is getting harder. But in Chengdu, female-only spaces are flourishing 
Read more 
It’s very difficult to imagine what happened during the MeToo period, she says, “when one survivor could speak publicly about her experience and trigger a broader discussion about sexual harassment.” 
On Friday Sophia Huang Xueqin the imprisoned journalist who helped to ignite China’s MeToo movement, was released from prison, five years after her arrest. She will return to see a feminist movement that has dramatically changed in the years she has been detained. 
In China feminism has become an increasingly private affair. Activists speak of a generational rupture. A movement once inspired by the global hashtag campaign against sexual abuse and harassment has retreated to a less public space. 
Across Chinese social media survivors post about sexual harassment and successful court cases online. But activists say hashtag campaigns like MeToo and its Chinese language equivalents have largely been scrubbed from the Chinese internet. 
View image in fullscreen 
Sophia Huang Xueqin. Photograph: Thomas Yau/SCMP/Getty Images 
“A lot of younger, digital-native feminists today don’t know much about those earlier feminist struggles not too long ago, thanks to the state’s intentional annihilation of them,” says Eva Liu, a researcher on Chinese feminism and digital media at Ohio University. 
Today, Chinese feminists employ creative ways to avoid censorship. They use new expressions to avoid posts being blocked. “It’s really a cat-and-mouse game,” says Liu. 
She describes an “encyclopaedia” of feminist words banned by Chinese censors. “There are staff specifically tasked with tracking new terms coined by feminists online and adding them to the keyword lists used for automated censorship,” she says. “Even some terms that are not yet popular among feminist users are already part of this automatic censorship list.” 
Li Sipan, a Chinese investigative journalist and feminist scholar, says: “The Chinese Communist party regards all mobilisation of the public and movements demanding changes from the government as threats. The feminist movement clearly has these characteristics.” 
Jasmine in Beijing says: “If you want to organise a public event, anything explicitly related to feminism or LGBT issues is basically not possible, at least in Beijing. If you advertise it that way, there’s a risk the event will be shut down. 
“So usually we frame the event in a more neutral way, without directly presenting it as being about gender or social issues. But once the event is taking place, we may still discuss those topics.” 
‘The online environment now is very different’
Huang’s reporting of survivors’ stories helped to propel the MeToo movement into public consciousness in China. She was arrested in 2021 in the city of Guangzhou a day before she was set to leave China to study a masters degree at Sussex University on a UK government-funded scholarship. 
View image in fullscreen 
Supporters hold banners in support of Zhou Xiaoxuan outside at a courthouse in 2020, who accused a TV presenter of sexual harassment. She later lost her legal case. Photograph: Andy Wong/AP 
In 2024 she was convicted alongside labour activist Wang Jianbing of “inciting subversion of state power”. 
Huang’s friends say they received little information about her from the authorities while she was in detention, amid reports of dramatic weight loss and intense interrogation, resulting in little sleep. Information travelled slowly out of the prison. They sometimes waited months for updates, relying on messages from other inmates who had been released. 
At the time of her conviction, Huang was also sentenced to four years “deprivation of political rights”. Human right groups say it could prevent her from continuing to work as a journalist or travelling abroad. 
In a statement released on Saturday, activists pushing for Huang’s release said “though she is released from prison, none of us [her friends] were able to reach her or receive any information from her. 
“Her whereabouts is also unknown. We are nervous and worried about her current conditions due to the potential severe surveillance she faces.” 
The Chinese government says the country has made “historic” progress in women’s rights. In a speech last year, president Xi Jinping listed improvements in health, employment and economic participation. China says it will further strengthen gender equality and protect against sexual harassment and sexual violence. 
Despite the shrinking space for debate, activists say the movement has had a lasting impact on Chinese society. Metoo made sexual harassment a mainstream topic. It led to policy change in universities, although activists say progress stopped at the courts. 
“I believe the achievements of China’s MeToo are things that many other authoritarian or even democratic countries failed to achieve,” says Lu Pin, a Chinese feminist activist, based in New York. “Under very harsh conditions, MeToo greatly raised women’s awareness of their rights, especially among young women.” 
View image in fullscreen 
Labour rights activist Wang Jianbing, who was convicted alongside Huang. Photograph: AP 
In Beijing, Jasmine hopes to meet Huang one day but is unsure if it will be possible. She says she is still in contact with survivors of sexual harassment and believes it’s possible to support them with publicity and legal support. 
She believes there are other individuals and groups offering similar help, but they must choose carefully how to effect change. “The online environment now is very different from when MeToo first emerged,” she says. 
Lu Pin agrees. “People used to have naive imaginations and expectations about the internet, but later realised it wasn’t like that, especially for women and feminism.”
